A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CapBencher, despite the changed title and presentation. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison; relocated material can be matched.

before.justification: v6 reports original controlled contamination, model-merging, reverse-engineering, multilingual, and pretraining experiments, including appendix results.

after.justification: v7 retains these original experiments and adds results on newer models, LEXam, accuracy reconstruction, and instruction-following violations.

M1.justification: The answer-randomization mechanism, binomial detector, original-accuracy estimator, and optional auditor remain. The auditor moves from Section 2.3 to Appendix B. Renaming concealment to obfuscation and clarifying release practices do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: v7 adds LEXam legal-exam data to the capped-versus-original evaluation, with results in Figure 17 and Table 5. The previously evaluated benchmarks, four task types, and multilingual scenarios remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated detector baselines remain the canary-string method, Min-k%, and Min-k%++. Reverse-engineering comparisons retain the same prompt methods and original-prompt reference. The additional LLMs expand evaluation configurations rather than the detector comparator set.

E3.justification: v7 adds Claude Sonnet 4.5 to tracking and GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5 mini, and GPT-5 nano to reverse-engineering evaluation. It also introduces reconstruction comparisons and output-violation metrics. Exact tracking sample sizes remain unclear: the new discussion uses full benchmark sizes, while Appendix D.4 retains the 1,024-example subsampling policy.

E4.justification: v7 substantially extends validation through empirical accuracy reconstruction in Figure 3, instruction-following checks across 77 model-benchmark setups in Table 13, and cap/sample-size sensitivity calculations in Table 14. Reverse-engineering robustness is also tested with four additional GPT variants. Earlier phrasing, reasoning, multilingual, and training-control analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds and mean/standard-deviation reporting, and retain the binomial and auditor t-tests. Table 14 supplies additional numerical illustrations of the existing variance formula, without introducing a different uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 2 and 9 retain Qwen results but add four GPT variants. New reconstruction results and Table 13's average violation rates of 0.9% and 0.1% substantially expand the findings. Table 5 adds LEXam's tau of 0.91 and changes aggregate tau from 0.93 to 0.92 under expanded coverage; v6's main text instead stated 0.96. The introductory NeurIPS author-count results are removed.

T1.justification: The substantive assumptions A1-A4, affine score relationship, variance theorem, and auditor derivations remain, with renumbering and notation clarification. The shortened corollary proof is equivalent, and Table 14 applies the existing variance theorem rather than introducing a new formal result.

C1.justification: The release, ranking, and contamination-detection contributions remain. The conclusion adds an explicit qualification that stronger future models may recover answers despite current reverse-engineering resistance. The increased emphasis on leaderboard hacking concerns a private-evaluation capability already claimed and tested in v6.

C2.justification: v7 explicitly warns that publishing reasoning exposes original answers, explains the leakage risk of repeatedly refreshing randomized answers, and discusses predictable seeds and stronger future attackers. It also adds concrete cap-selection recommendations and interprets ranking instability on small benchmarks. These refine limitations already partly acknowledged in v6.

D1.justification: v7 adds access links for CapBencher's training/evaluation implementation and capped datasets. Appendix F newly documents manual capping of MATH-500 versus automated capping elsewhere and provides release instructions. Existing hardware and baseline implementation information is retained in the relocated reproducibility statement.

R1.justification: v7 adds references including LEXam, Misaki and Akiba's probabilistic-prompting work, and OpenAI's SWE-bench discussion, while removing Mohri et al. The established positioning against contamination detectors, label noise, and dynamic evaluation largely remains; Appendix A adds a limited comparison with refreshing randomized answers.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively revised around test-set overfitting. The method exposition is streamlined, the auditor and reproducibility statement move to appendices, and a practical-recommendations appendix is added. This substantially changes the narrative and organization.

P2.justification: v7 adopts a two-column main-text layout and rearranges the overview figure. It removes the author-count chart, expands the main ranking display, adds a reconstruction figure, enlarges the reverse-engineering tables with model groups and underlining, and adds Tables 13-14. Numerous retained displays are resized or relocated.

improvement.justification: The reconstruction and assumption checks, broader attacker evaluation, clearer disclosure limitations, and new code/data access information make the retained method easier to assess and use. These provide a limited net improvement. Reporting inconsistencies temper the gains, particularly the new full-size explanation of ranking stability alongside the retained subsampling policy.
